title: Improving the Spatiotemporal Resolution in Light-sheet Fluorescence Microscopy
content: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) has generated significant interest in biological research as a result of its ability to volumetrically image biological specimens with high optical sectioning and low photobleaching and phototoxicity. While its imaging speed can be high, the spatial resolution is often modest, as the numerical aperture of the used objectives is limited. This is due to the orthogonal arrangement of illumination and detection objectives, which have to split the available solid angle. Typically, a numerical aperture of 1.1 or less is used for detection, which limits the sensitivity and lateral resolution in LSFM. Furthermore, the orthogonal imaging geometry sterically occludes many commonly used sample mounting methods (e.g., microfluidics and multi-well plates), and typically one cannot freely change the objectives to adapt the system to different imaging tasks.
